 Advertisement Advertisement Gold’s Rebound Needs 2 Things — A Fed Catalyst and a $4,106 Breakout
 By Fawad Razaqzada Commodities Published 10/28/2026, 01:51 PM Gold’s Rebound Needs 2 Things — A Fed Catalyst and a $4,106 Breakout View all comments (1) 1 Gold’s Rebound Needs 2 Things — A Fed Catalyst and a $4,106 Breakout View all comments (1) 1 Fawad Razaqzada Articles ( 631 ) | My Homepage Follow In this article: Gold Spot US Dollar -0.56% GC -0.05% 
 Gold is stabilising near $4,000, but the broader downtrend remains intact.
 Higher oil prices, inflation risks and elevated bond yields are limiting recovery, while central-bank buying offers longer-term support.
 Gold needs to reclaim $4,075–$4,106 to signal improving momentum; failure could expose the summer low near $3,942.

 Gold prices eased back overnight, giving up some of Tuesday’s gains as the metal continues to hover around the $4,000 level. After last week’s 4% sell-off briefly took gold below this psychological threshold, the metal has at least managed to stabilise in the first couple of sessions this week.
 The question now is whether this is the start of a more meaningful recovery or simply a pause in the broader correction. Gold needs to show that sellers are genuinely losing control before the short-term outlook can turn decisively more bullish.
 All Eyes on the Fed 
 With some stability returning to the AI trade, markets have been able to refocus on what is arguably the more immediate macro threat: higher energy prices, renewed inflation pressure and what that means for monetary policy.
 Despite September’s hotter-than-expected inflation data and renewed concerns about price pressures, the Fed is widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged today. The more interesting question is what policymakers signal about the next move.
 The market’s rapid pricing-out of an October rate hike was somewhat surprising given the strength of the September CPI report, which initially pushed the probability of a hike above 50%. But comments from Fed officials including Philip Jefferson, Michelle Bowman and Christopher Waller subsequently suggested there was little urgency to tighten policy further, helping to calm those expectations.
 For gold, however, the underlying problem has not disappeared. Higher oil prices risk keeping inflation elevated, which could force central banks to maintain restrictive policy for longer. That keeps bond yields relatively attractive and raises the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset such as gold.
 This is one reason the metal has struggled to sustain its rebounds.
 Why Isn’t Gold Bouncing More Strongly? 
 Gold is being pulled in opposite directions by the same macro force: inflation.
 Persistent inflation should, in theory, support demand for gold as a store of value and hedge against the erosion of purchasing power. But if inflation proves sticky enough to keep central banks hawkish, rising nominal and real yields work against the metal.
 That tension has become increasingly important as oil prices have surged again. Investors can still earn relatively attractive returns from government bonds, making it harder for gold to compete in the short term despite its longer-term appeal.
 This helps explain why even relatively sharp intraday recoveries have failed to develop into sustained rallies.
 There is, however, another side to the equation.
 Central Banks Provide a Structural Floor 
 Central-bank buying remains an important source of demand that is less sensitive to short-term movements in bond yields. Purchases from countries including China have helped provide a structural underpinning for the gold market, reinforcing the longer-term argument for holding the metal.
 That does not mean central-bank demand will prevent further declines. But it does make the case for a prolonged bear market less convincing.
 If investors believe official-sector buying will remain strong, sizeable dips may become increasingly attractive to longer-term buyers through the physical, ETF and futures markets. In other words, central-bank accumulation could help put a floor under gold even while the near-term macro backdrop remains challenging.
 Gold has already fallen nearly 30% from its January peak, while silver has suffered an even sharper correction of around 55%. Silver has now broken below its summer lows and moved deep into a long-term support zone between $50 and $55.
 Gold, by contrast, has so far held above its summer low around $3,942.
 After such sizeable declines, both metals are arguably becoming increasingly vulnerable to a counter-trend bounce. But for gold, I would still want to see a bullish trigger before turning more constructive.
 Gold Still Needs to Prove Sellers Are Losing Control 
 The metal has found some support around $4,000 over the past couple of sessions, but the technical picture remains bearish until we see a meaningful higher high. 
 Gold has managed only two weekly gains over the past nine weeks, highlighting just how persistent the selling pressure has been. That momentum makes it difficult to argue that a durable bottom is already in place.
 That said, markets rarely move in straight lines, and I would not be surprised to see gold carve out a bottom around current levels.
 The first important test on any rebound comes around $4,075-$4,106. This was an important support area and the base of the rally that began in early August. Having broken below it, the zone could now turn into resistance.
 A sustained move back above $4,075-$4,106 would therefore be significant. It would suggest that sellers are struggling to defend the breakdown and that the recent sell-off may have run its course.
 A decisive break above the descending trend line connecting the recent highs would provide another, stronger signal that momentum is turning.
 Until then, I would treat rallies with some caution. Gold may be close to finding a floor, but it still needs to prove it.
